title: Ang 8: Japji ends, So Dar begins
hookLine: the last salok, then the first evening hymns
tomorrow: who's speaking when the evening hymns change voice?
last: A CLEAN PLACE · ALOUD AND SILENT · READ TOGETHER.

cards: Some phones slip into a darker screen at sunset on their own, no button pressed. The day hands over to the evening and you barely notice the seam. Ang eight has a seam like that, on paper.
Near the top, the morning prayer is finishing. Lower down, a new heading appears, and the evening has started.

teach.h: AIR, WATER, EARTH: THE LAST SALOK.
teach.b: The Japji closes with a salok. In the original: pavan guroo paanee pitaa maataa dharat mahat. Air is the Guru, water the father, earth the great mother.

teach.h: DAY AND NIGHT, THE TWO NURSES.
teach.b: Then, in paraphrase, day and night are the two nurses, and the whole world plays in their lap. A few lines later the Japji is done.

And on the same page comes a new heading, raga Asa, and the first of the evening hymns: So Dar. It opens with a question, in paraphrase: what is that door, what is that house, where you sit and care for all?

Something to tell someone tonight: the Japji's last salok names day and night as the world's two nurses, and on that very page the evening hymns begin. The morning and the evening prayers aren't in two books.

how: Sikhs say the Japji in the morning and the Rehras in the evening; in the Guru Granth Sahib the Japji ends on ang 8, where So Dar, the first hymns of the evening prayer, begin.

o: the eighth hymn of the Sohila, said at night

games.q: Maya wants to read just the morning prayer from the Granth on her own. where do you tell her to stop?
o: at the end of the last salok, before the new heading for So Dar.
at the bottom of ang 8; the whole page is the Japji.
after the first page; the rest is commentary on it.
games.why: the Japji closes with its salok on ang 8, and a new heading begins So Dar, the evening hymns, on the same page. the heading tells you.

practice: Listen to one sound: your own breath, the air the salok calls the Guru. Don't change it; just hear it come in and go out, like day handing over to night.
If you have the page in front of you, rest your eyes on the place where the Japji ends and So Dar begins.
